IT'S INSANE WHAT GROK CAN DO

I GAVE GROK BOT $75. FIVE HOURS LATER, THE BALANCE WAS $4,800.

64× the starting balance in one session. That's my result from this run.

But a balance screenshot leaves out the part that matters: how a trade gets permission to happen.

The useful way to think about an agent desk is five separate jobs:

→ SCOUT — find wallets worth investigating. A profitable exit gets a wallet onto a research list; it doesn't automatically make its next entry worth copying.
→ FILTER — check concentration, liquidity, developer holdings and suspicious activity. Missing data should stop the process.
→ ANALYST — examine what survived. Is there still an opportunity at the price available now?
→ EXECUTOR — translate an approved decision into a bounded order. Position size and execution price matter.
→ GUARD — check exposure and exit conditions before the order is allowed through.

In a desk built this way, every role needs a record: the input it saw, the check it ran and the decision it passed on.

I'd judge that workflow by the trades it takes and the signals it rejects, with a reason I can inspect afterward.

For the next run, the evidence I want is simple:
• Every entry and exit, with timestamps.
• Fees and the difference between the expected price and the fill.
• Realized P&L separated from open positions.
• The reason each order passed or failed.

$75 → $4,800 is one five-hour outcome. It doesn't establish a repeatable return.

note_tweet.text:
Stop making Grok Bot relearn a job you already taught it

Stripe demonstrated the payoff: one integration task took roughly 20 engineering days with plain Claude Code and 4 with reusable prompts.

Build that discipline into Grok Bot:

1. Give an Operator Bot one recurring job and a clear definition of done.

2. Save each proven step as a skill with inputs, validation checks, expected output and approval rules.

3. Give a Reviewer Bot the output, source links and run notes. Ask it to flag missing evidence, repeated investigations and failed tools.

4. Review its proposed skill edits, test them on a fresh example, then schedule the workflow.

Private skills can be reused across your Bots. A routine decides when the work runs.

For a competitor brief, let one Bot gather changes and another check every claim against its source.

Measure correction count, review time and repeated tool failures to see whether the workflow is improving.

I PUT A GROK BOT NIGHT DESK  ACCOUNT WITH $37.19 AND WENT TO BED. BY 7AM IT READ $8,904.62, WITH A WHY NEXT TO EVERY TRADE

I spent months asking chat models "would you buy this?" and scrolling through maybes. this weekend I described a desk to Grok Bot instead. it built the whole thing, I didn't write a line of code

six agents, one screen, one rule each:

> spotter: points at fresh pairs, never buys
> safety gate: no pass, no order. it blocked 23 tokens overnight
> risk: size moves with the balance, never a fixed ticket
> trader: walks away above 2% slip
> scribe: no line without a why
> ledger: books every close, redraws the curve

at 7am the journal had 148 lines. 19 losing trades right next to the 42 winners, each with its reason

that's the shift. I stopped asking the chat what it would do and started reading what already happened
